description: In the Norse sky, warrior women choose the dead who will fill Valhalla. Their army has to face the twilight of the gods.

hero.hook: Dying with a sword in your hand is not an ending: it is a selection for the last war of the world.

blocks.text: In Norse mythology, death in battle is not an ending. It is a **selection**. The **Valkyries**, whose name means “those who choose the slain,” ride over the battlefields for Odin, the sovereign god.

Their mission is to carry the bravest to **Valhalla**, the “hall of the slain.” That palace is not a paradise of rest. It is a barracks in the sky. Odin is raising an army for [[Ragnarök]], the final battle that will destroy the world and kill the gods.

**Odin** knows the prophecy. At [[Ragnarök]], the giants and the monsters will fall on [[Asgard]], the home of the gods. To delay the inevitable he needs elite soldiers: the **Einherjar**, “those who fight alone.”

blocks.caption: Odin, master of the gods, haunted by the end of the world

blocks.text: Valhalla took in only **half** of the warriors who fell in battle. The other half went to Fólkvangr, the realm of the goddess **Freyja**. Even after a heroic death, the heroes were split.

Valhalla, in Asgard, has **540 doors**. Each one is wide enough for eight hundred fighters to pass side by side. Only those who fell bravely, sword in hand, have the right to enter. The Valkyries do the sorting from the sky.

The modern picture of the Valkyries often comes from the romanticism of the 19th century: gentle maidens on horseback. The old texts, such as the [[Poetic Edda]], paint far harsher figures. They are tied to ravens, the birds of corpses. Some poems show them as grim spinners whose threads are entrails and whose weights are heads.

blocks.caption: A Valkyrie in flight: Odin's messenger and supplier of heroes

blocks.text: Figures like **Brynhildr** or [[Sigrun]] also have a human face. They waver between Odin's orders and their feelings for mortals. In Valhalla their role changes. They set aside their armor to serve mead to the heroes. The gesture is a mark of respect: the brave dead man has become the elite of Asgard.

sections.title: Warrior women darker than we think

blocks.text: In Valhalla there is no quiet retirement. At the crow of the rooster [[Gullinkambi]], the Einherjar arm themselves and kill each other on the plain of [[Idavoll]]. In the evening the wounds close. The dead get up again. Then comes the feast.

blocks.caption: The feast of the Einherjar: battle by day, banquets by night

blocks.text: The boar **Sæhrímnir** is boiled every day by the cook [[Andhrímnir]], then comes back to life. Mead flows from the udders of the goat [[Heidrun]]. The Viking paradise is a permanent training ground.
This cycle of violence and pleasure binds Odin's army together. Centuries of friendly battles before the real enemy.

sections.title: Fight every day, feast every night

blocks.text: This view of the afterlife shaped Viking Scandinavia. Physical courage was prized. Dying of old age or illness, the “straw death,” led to **Hel**, a dull realm. Better to fall with weapons in hand.

The Valkyrie has crossed the centuries. Richard Wagner fixed her in European memory with [[The Ride of the Valkyries]]. Today she has become an archetype of the powerful woman, often far from her first job: supplying corpses to a god who is preparing his own end.
The **Valkyries** recruit the best of the dead for **Valhalla**. There the Einherjar fight and feast endlessly, with [[Ragnarök]] in view. The Norse paradise is a barracks, not a refuge.

sections.title: A worthy death rather than a “straw death”
